latin: Adulēscēns quīdam amīcum rogat nōnne<sup>1</sup> sibi<sup>2</sup> auxilium ferre possit.
In viīs suburbānīs<sup>3</sup> obscūrīsque prōgrediuntur<sup>4</sup>, dōnec<sup>5</sup> adulēscēns equum carpentō jūnctum<sup>6</sup> amīcō ostendit<sup>7</sup>.
Oportet equum disjungāmus et ad domum quamdam perdūcāmus.
Equum disjungunt<sup>8</sup> et ad domum dictam perveniunt.
Nūllum est hīc<sup>9</sup> stabulum<sup>10</sup>! Quō equum dūcere dēbēmus?
Ad tabulātum quīntum. Haec est ratiō cūr ā tē auxilium petierim<sup>11</sup>. Nihil tamen timuerīs: adest scānsōrium pēgma<sup>12</sup>.
Amīcus mīrātur. Nihilōminus auxilium fert atque ambō<sup>13</sup> nōn sine multō sūdōre equum in pēgmate collocant.
Amīcō et equō in cellā inclūsīs<sup>14</sup> (trēs persōnās cellā capere nōn poterat) adulēscēns ad tabulātum quīntum gradibus ascendit et inde scansōriō electrīcō pulsōriō attollit.
latinAccented: Adulḗscēns quīdam amī́cum rogat nōnne<sup>1</sup> sibi<sup>2</sup> auxílium ferre possit.
In viīs suburbā́nīs<sup>3</sup> obscūrī́sque prōgrediúntur<sup>4</sup>, dōnec<sup>5</sup> adulḗscēns equum carpéntō jūnctum<sup>6</sup> amī́cō osténdit<sup>7</sup>.
Opórtet equum disjungā́mus et ad domum quamdam perdūcā́mus.
Equum disjúngunt<sup>8</sup> et ad domum dictam pervéniunt.
Nūllum est hīc<sup>9</sup> stábulum<sup>10</sup>! Quō equum dū́cere dēbḗmus?
Ad tabulā́tum quīntum. Haec est rátiō cūr ā tē auxílium petíerim<sup>11</sup>. Nihil tamen timúerīs: adest scānsṓrium pēgma<sup>12</sup>.
Amī́cus mīrā́tur. Nihilṓminus auxílium fert atque ambō<sup>13</sup> nōn sine multō sūdṓre equum in pḗgmate cóllocant.
Amī́cō et equō in cellā inclū́sīs<sup>14</sup> (trēs persṓnās cellā cápere nōn póterat) adulḗscēns ad tabulā́tum quīntum grádibus ascéndit et inde scansṓriō electrī́cō pulsṓriō attóllit.
english: A certain young man asks a friend whether he could not [do him a favour] (to himself help bring).
[As] the other agreed, he [said to him] (said): “Come with me!”
They advance in the dark (and) suburban streets until the young man [shows his friend] a horse harnessed to a cab (a horse to a cab yoked to the friend shows).
We must unhitch the horse and lead [it] to a certain house.
They unhitch the horse and arrive at the house [indicated] (said).
There is no stable here! Where must we lead the horse?
To the fifth floor. That is the reason why I asked you for help. However, [don't] be afraid (subj. pft) [of] anything: there is a lift (cf. note).
The friend is astonished. Nevertheless [he gives his] help (he brings) and [the two of them] (the one and the other) settle the horse in the lift not without [much] (a lot of) sweat.

[His] friend and the horse having been shut in the cabin (the cabin could not take three people), the young man climbs the stairs to the fifth floor and from there [calls] the lift with the electric [button] (push-button raises).

footnotes: Nonne: this word, which you have already seen in DIRECT QUESTIONS (nonne venis?, aren't you coming?) is found again in INDIRECT QUESTIONS: te rogo nonne venias, I ask you whether you are not coming. In the indirect question the SUBJUNCTIVE is used, NEVER THE INDICATIVE.

Sibi, dative of the reflexive pronoun (acc. se; gen. sui, abl. se), corresponds to mihi, tibi (acc. me, te; gen. mei, tui). This pronoun, which cannot be a subject (except in an infinitive clause, as it has no nominative, unlike ego and tu), REFERS TO THE SUBJECT; if it is found, as here, in a subordinate clause, it refers to the subject of the main clause when the subordinate represents the thought of that subject (here adulescens).
Urbs, urbis, f., gen. pl. urbium, the city (with a capital U: Rome). Urbanus, -a, -um, urban (relating to the city); sub, under; whence suburbanus, suburban, of the suburbs (cf. English suburb).
Progredior, -eris, -i, -gressus sum, to advance, to progress. We already had ingredior, to enter. Pro, in front or instead of...
Jungo, -is, -ere, junxi, junctum, to join, that is to harness to the yoke (jugum, -i, n.).
Ostendo, -is, -ere, ostendi, ostensum (or ostentum), to show (ostensibly).
Disjungere = dis (idea of separation) + jungere (vid. sup. N. 5).

Hic is here an adverb derived from the adjective-pronoun we saw yesterday. Likewise we have istic and illic. All three designate the place one is showing: the first corresponds to the 1st person (hic: in the place that I am showing); the second likewise to the 2nd person and the last to the 3rd. Finally ibi, there, corresponds to the place just spoken of. All of them answer the question ubi?, where? (without movement).
Stabulum, -i, n., gave French étable (cowshed), but rather corresponds to the stable.

Cur a te auxilium petivi?, Why did I ask you for help? In the direct question the verb is in the indicative. In sentence 7 the same interrogative adverb cur is used for the indirect question (vid. sup. N. 1). The verb petere (peto, -is, -ere, -ii, petitum) is then in the subjunctive (perfect). A te, from you (abl.) and not tibi, for you (dat.).
Pegma, -atis, n. (3rd declension), scaffolding, lifting machine, of Greek origin. Scansorius, -a, -um, relating to climbing; from scando, -is, -ere, scandi, scansum, to climb.
Ambo, m., f., ambae, n., ambo, both.

Amico et equo inclusis. This construction is called the ABLATIVE ABSOLUTE; literally: the friend and the horse having been shut in. The whole is equivalent to an adverbial clause. Note at the same time the rule of agreement: amico and equo are in the ablative singular, but as 1 + 1 = 2, inclusis is in the ablative plural.

latin: Id libentissimē accipiam, sed nesciō ubi sit domus tua.
Est in viā Portuāriā numerō decimō septimō (distīncta), tabulātō octāvō, jānuā alterā sinistrōrsum.
Eam facile inveniēs: incipit ante statiōnem ferriviāriam et ad portum dūcit.
Minimē! Nōn amplius quam trecenta metra.
Optimē! Crās igitur tē revīsam. Valē!
latinAccented: Id libentíssimē accípiam, sed nésciō ubi sit domus tua.
Est in viā Portuā́riā númerō décimō séptimō (distī́ncta), tabulā́tō octā́vō, jā́nuā álterā sinistrṓrsum.
Eam fácile invéniēs: íncipit ante statiṓnem ferriviā́riam et ad portum dūcit.
Mínimē! Nōn ámplius quam trecénta metra.
Óptimē! Crās ígitur tē revī́sam. Valē!
english: Do you want to have lunch at [my] house tomorrow?
I would accept [that] with the greatest pleasure, but I don't know where your house is (subj.).
It's [in] Harbour Street (Port street) [number] 17 (distinguished by number 17), [on the] 8th floor, 2nd door on the left.
You will find it easily: it begins at the (railway) station and leads to the harbour.
Is it far from the station?
Not at all! No more than 300 m.
Perfect! I shall see you again tomorrow, then. [Goodbye] (be well)!
